question.text: A company listed on BSE has 1 crore total shares outstanding. In the preceding 12 months, 12 lakh shares were traded. An acquirer triggers an open offer. How should the offer price be determined?

answer.text: At the highest of the parameters specified under Regulation 8, including the VWAP of the 60 trading days preceding the relevant date, as the shares are frequently traded
Simply at the VWAP of 30 trading days preceding the relevant date
Through independent valuation, as the shares are infrequently traded
At the book value per share as determined by the latest audited financials

explanation.text: The Logic: Shares are classified as "frequently traded" if the annualised traded turnover during the preceding 12 calendar months is at least 10% of the total number of shares. Here, 12 lakh out of 1 crore = 12%, so the shares are frequently traded. The open offer price is then the HIGHEST of the parameters listed under Regulation 8 of the SAST Regulations, one of which (for frequently traded shares) is the volume-weighted average market price for 60 trading days preceding the relevant date. The Trap: A common mistake is to read "frequently traded" as fixing the price at the 60-day VWAP alone. The 60-day VWAP is only one of several Regulation 8 parameters; the offer price must be the highest of all applicable parameters (including the negotiated price under the share-purchase agreement, the highest price paid by the acquirer in the 52 weeks preceding the public announcement, etc.). Note: If the shares had been infrequently traded, the 60-day VWAP parameter would have been replaced by a price determined by the acquirer and the manager to the offer taking into account valuation parameters such as book value, comparable trading multiples and other relevant factors.
